analysis.one_liner: Eases proof standards for older black lung disability claims by disabled coal miners.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: it sat in a House subcommittee from February 1993 until the Congress ended in January 1995, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the federal Black Lung Benefits Program to make it easier for a specific group of coal miners to win disability benefits: miners with at least 10 years in the mines who filed claims between July 1973 and April 1980. Under the bill, any single qualifying piece of medical evidence — one positive chest X-ray, one set of positive breathing tests, one set of blood gas tests, or a physician's documented opinion — would be enough to create a presumption that the miner is totally disabled due to black lung disease from coal mining. No higher standard of proof would be allowed. This closed a gap for miners whose claims were judged under stricter rules adopted in 1980, many of whom had the disease but could not prove it to the government's satisfaction.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with at least 10 years of mining employment whose black lung claims were filed between July 1, 1973, and April 1, 1980, and the surviving families of miners who died in that period. For these claimants, a single piece of qualifying medical evidence would have triggered a legal presumption of total disability from pneumoconiosis, dramatically lowering the burden of proof that had denied many of them benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older coal miners with black lung disease

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required the government to presume that a miner with 10 or more years of coal mining employment who filed a claim between July 1, 1973, and April 1, 1980, is or was totally disabled due to pneumoconiosis — or, for a deceased miner, that the death was due to the disease — if any one of four medical conditions is met [S3].

Qualifying evidence would include a single positive chest X-ray, biopsy, or autopsy; a single set of positive breathing (ventilatory) studies; a single set of positive blood gas studies showing impaired oxygen transfer; or other medical evidence including a physician's documented opinion [S3].

The bill stated that nothing in it could be construed to require proof of the medical condition by a preponderance of the evidence or any higher standard, meaning one qualifying exhibit would suffice to invoke the presumption [S3].

The target window matters because it runs to April 1, 1980 — the date federal regulations tightened the medical evidence required to prove black lung total disability, which is why claims from that earlier period were judged under rules many miners could not meet; the bill's stated purpose was to give those older claims a presumption of eligibility [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Black Lung Benefits Program, which is financed largely by excise taxes on coal production and, in some claims, coal mine operators themselves, would bear the cost of newly presumed benefits for this group of older claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal operators and the black lung trust fund

drawbacks.text: The bill set a deliberately low bar: a single positive X-ray or one physician's opinion would trigger a presumption of total disability without any requirement to prove the condition by a preponderance of the evidence, which critics of such presumptions argue pays some claimants whose breathing impairment does not actually prevent all work [S3].

The relief was narrow by design — it covered only miners with 10+ years of employment whose claims were filed between July 1, 1973, and April 1, 1980 — so similarly situated miners with claims filed after April 1, 1980 would get no help from this bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the covered group the benefit is substantial: it would have converted an evidentiary standard that denied many miners into a single-piece-of-evidence presumption, likely converting denials into monthly benefit awards. The cost falls on a defined financing base — the coal excise tax that funds black lung benefits and, in some claims, coal operators — and is bounded by the size of the covered claim cohort. The main design trade-off is accuracy versus ease of proof: paying on one positive X-ray will include some claimants a stricter standard would screen out, which is precisely why such presumptions are used for occupational diseases where X-rays and breathing tests understate true disease.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, sent to its Labor Standards subcommittee on February 11, 1993, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Kanjorski (D-PA) introduced the bill on January 26, 1993 [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
On February 11, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety, where it remained [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action — appears in the record through the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators and the black lung financing system were spared the added benefit liability the presumption would have created; the miners with 1973-1980 claims got nothing and their claims remain judged under the stricter standards.

for.name: Rep. Paul Kanjorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 26, 1993, to establish a black lung disability presumption for older claims.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor action
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from referral on January 26, 1993, through the end of the Congress without acting on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety
against.role: Subcommittee of referral; never took the bill up
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 11, 1993, and took no further recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and it never reached a vote, so no record shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Had the bill passed, operators and the coal-funded Black Lung trust fund would have faced more benefit awards for older claims, since a single positive X-ray or breathing test would have presumed total disability. Blocking the bill kept those costs off the industry's books, while miners with disease continued to go unpaid.

The Black Lung Benefits Program is financed in significant part by excise taxes on coal production; a failed benefits expansion means the industry's funding obligation for this older cohort of claims did not grow.
